message.content: We will prove it NP-complete. First, we show that it belongs to NP. A certificate simply lists the subgraph's vertices and edges for checking. Verifying that the weight equals k takes polynomial time in the overall input size. Now, we formally demonstrate NP-hardness by constructing a polynomial-time reduction from the classical Partition problem instance below. Given Partition instance with n positive integers summing to target T, we build a graph G with n extra vertices. The star graph has center vertex c of weight zero and leaf vertices v1 through vn each with weights a1 through an respectively. Every single edge connecting the center vertex c to any leaf vertex vi carries weight zero, and we set target value k to T over two. If some subset I of the indices satisfies the condition that the sum of ai for i in I equals T over two, then the Partition instance is yes. The corresponding subgraph S uses the vertex set containing center c together with every leaf vi where i is in I, and it includes absolutely no edges at all in the construction. The total weight of this subgraph S is zero from the center vertex c plus the sum of all weights ai for all indices i in the set I, which equals T over two exactly. Conversely, if G contains some subgraph of total weight k equal to T over two, then the set of leaf vertices included in that subgraph gives a subset I with the exact required sum of T over two. This subset I partitions the original integer set into two perfectly balanced groups, where group I has sum T over two and the complement group has the identical sum T over two, proving that the Partition instance is a yes instance. The reduction clearly and efficiently runs in polynomial time because we merely create the simple star graph structure and directly assign all the vertex and edge weights from the given input integers, performing absolutely no complicated arithmetic whatsoever in the entire reduction process overall. Therefore, the original Partition instance is a yes instance if and only if the graph G contains a subgraph of total weight exactly equal to k, which fully completes the NP-hardness proof and thereby formally establishes the NP-completeness of the SUBGRAPH WEIGHT decision problem in its entirety.
